# Appendix C: Statistical model {#sec-app-model}

For repetition $i$, let $B_i$ and $C_i$ be the baseline and candidate measurements, $r_i$ the centered repetition position, and $o_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ the run-order contrast indicating which branch was run first. Let $z_B=-1$ and $z_C=+1$ identify the baseline and candidate measurements within each pair.

A simple model for the two measurements is

$$
y_{ik}
=
\mu
+
\frac{z_k}{2}
\left(
\Delta+\Delta_r r_i+\Delta_o o_i
\right)
+
\varepsilon_{ik}.
$$

Here, $\mu$ is the midpoint of the baseline and candidate measurements. The $\Delta$ coefficients describe the candidate-minus-baseline effect. $\Delta$ is the effect at $r=o=0$, while $\Delta_r$ and $\Delta_o$ describe how that effect changes with repetition position and run order.

The $1/2$ makes the $\Delta$ coefficients direct candidate-minus-baseline contrasts. In particular,

$$
E[C_i-B_i]
=
\Delta+\Delta_r r_i+\Delta_o o_i.
$$

The full model also allows the level shared by the baseline and candidate to vary with repetition position and run order:

$$
y_{ik}
=
\mu+\mu_r r_i+\mu_o o_i
+
\frac{z_k}{2}
\left(
\Delta+\Delta_r r_i+\Delta_o o_i
\right)
+
\varepsilon_{ik}.
$$

The $\mu_r$ and $\mu_o$ coefficients are nuisance terms. They account for changes that affect the baseline and candidate equally, while the corresponding $\Delta$ coefficients describe changes in the candidate-minus-baseline effect.

`foil` fits this model through its equivalent midpoint and difference regressions. Define

$$
m_i=\frac{B_i+C_i}{2},
\qquad
d_i=C_i-B_i.
$$

Then

$$
m_i
=
\mu+\mu_r r_i+\mu_o o_i+\varepsilon_i^{(m)},
$$

and

$$
d_i
=
\Delta+\Delta_r r_i+\Delta_o o_i+\varepsilon_i^{(d)}.
$$

Thus the midpoint regression estimates the shared level, while the difference regression estimates the candidate-minus-baseline effect. A disturbance shared by both measurements in a pair cancels from $d_i$.

For each Bayesian-bootstrap draw, `foil` samples one weight for each pair,

$$
w_i \sim \operatorname{Exp}(1),
$$

and fits both regressions by weighted least squares using the same weights. Normalizing these weights gives

$$
\left(
\frac{w_1}{\sum_j w_j},
\dots,
\frac{w_n}{\sum_j w_j}
\right)
\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1),
$$

so this is the standard Bayesian bootstrap [@rubinBayesianBootstrap1981]. Using the same pair weights for both regressions preserves their joint uncertainty.

The fitted intercepts give the adjusted baseline and candidate values at $r=o=0$:

$$
\mu_B
=
\hat{\mu}-\frac{\hat{\Delta}}{2},
\qquad
\mu_C
=
\hat{\mu}+\frac{\hat{\Delta}}{2}.
$$
Shrinkage, when requested, acts only on the candidate-minus-baseline effect. The parameter $\lambda$ represents a prior count of zero difference pseudo-observations. For $\lambda=0$, the model above is unchanged. Since each observed pair has expected weight $E[w_i]=1$ while the pseudo-observation has expected weight $E[g]=\lambda$, $\lambda$ can be interpreted as the effective prior sample size for zero difference. For $\lambda>0$, each Bayesian-bootstrap draw additionally samples

$$
g \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(\lambda,1)
$$

and adds a zero difference pseudo-observation at $r=o=0$ with weight $g$. Equivalently, the difference regression minimizes

$$
\sum_i
w_i
\left(
d_i-\Delta-\Delta_r r_i-\Delta_o o_i
\right)^2
+
g\Delta^2
$$

while the midpoint regression is unaffected.
